q: You're driving slowly up a long, steep hill and several vehicles behind want to overtake. There's a climbing lane on your left. What should you do?
options: Use the climbing lane to let them pass
Stay in the main lane and speed up
Stop on the hill so they can get by
Switch on your hazard warning lights
explain: Climbing and crawler lanes are provided on some hills. Use the lane if you're driving a slow-moving vehicle or if there are vehicles behind you wishing to overtake, and watch for signs that it's about to end.

q: You're driving down a long, steep hill. Why shouldn't you rely only on the footbrake to control your speed?
options: It will make your tyres lose pressure
It can cause the engine to overheat
Heavy use can reduce its effectiveness
It will drain the battery quickly
explain: Increased use of the footbrake can reduce its effectiveness. Select a lower gear before you reach a long downhill slope and don't coast, so engine braking helps you control your speed.

q: You're approaching a right-hand bend on a two-way road. Where should you position your car?
options: Well to the left
Close to the centre line
Straddling the centre line
As far right as is safe
explain: Keep well to the left on right-hand bends. This will improve your view of the road and help avoid the risk of colliding with traffic approaching from the opposite direction.

q: You're driving along a winding road. Why should you keep both hands on the steering wheel where possible?
options: To make the steering feel lighter
To stop the airbag from activating
To show other drivers you're alert
To remain in full control of the car
explain: Drive with both hands on the wheel where possible. This will help you to remain in full control of the vehicle at all times.

q: You're in a listed self-driving vehicle with its self-driving function switched on. It prompts you to take back control. What MUST you do?
options: Let it carry on driving itself
Wait until the end of the journey
Ignore it unless the road is busy
Take control when it prompts you
explain: If a self-driving vehicle needs to hand control back to you, it will give you enough warning. You MUST always be able and ready to take control, and do it when the vehicle prompts you, so stay in the driving seat and stay awake.

q: You're coming to a normal stop at traffic lights. What's the safest way to brake?
options: Early and lightly, then more firmly
Late and hard, then release it
Pump the brake pedal on and off
Handbrake first, then footbrake
explain: In normal circumstances, the safest way to brake is early and lightly. Brake more firmly as you begin to stop, then ease the pressure off just before the vehicle comes to rest to avoid a jerky stop.

q: You've just driven through a flooded section of road where the water was deep. What should you do at the first safe opportunity?
options: Check your tyre pressures
Gently test your brakes
Rev the engine to dry it
Check your oil level
explain: If you've driven through deep water your brakes may be less effective. Test them at the first safe opportunity by pushing gently on the brake pedal to make sure that they work.

q: You're driving on a narrow country road with lots of bends. Why should you reduce your speed as you approach each bend?
options: Bends can be sharper than they appear
Country roads have lower speed limits
Your tyres grip less on country roads
Speed cameras are often placed on bends
explain: Take extra care on country roads and reduce your speed at approaches to bends, which can be sharper than they appear. Make sure you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

q: You're driving along a country road and approaching a village. What should you do?
options: Keep to the speed you used on the open road
Speed up to get through the village quickly
Use main beam to warn people you're coming
Reduce your speed as you enter the village
explain: You should reduce your speed where country roads enter villages. On country roads, be prepared for pedestrians, horse riders, cyclists, slow-moving farm vehicles or mud on the road.

q: You're on a single-track road and see a car coming towards you. The nearest passing place is on your right. What should you do?
options: Pull into the passing place on your right
Wait opposite the passing place
Flash your headlights and carry on
Drive onto the verge on your left
explain: On single-track roads, if you see a vehicle coming towards you, pull into a passing place on your left, or wait opposite a passing place on your right.

q: Your car doesn't have anti-lock brakes. A child runs out in front of you and you have to stop in an emergency. What should you try to avoid?
options: Braking as soon as you see the hazard
Braking so hard that the wheels lock
Keeping both hands on the steering wheel
Holding the car straight as you stop
explain: In an emergency, brake immediately. Try to avoid braking so harshly that you lock your wheels, as locked wheels can lead to loss of control.

q: You're driving downhill on a narrow single-track road. A vehicle is coming uphill towards you. What should you do?
options: Give way to it whenever you can
Expect it to reverse for you
Flash your headlights to claim priority
Keep going, as downhill has priority
explain: Give way to road users coming uphill whenever you can. If necessary, reverse until you reach a passing place to let the other vehicle pass.

q: You're driving on a single-track road and want to stop for a break. What does the Highway Code say about passing places?
options: You may park in them for up to an hour
You shouldn't park in them
You may park in them in daylight
You may park in ones on your left
explain: Do not park in passing places. They're there so vehicles can pass each other or let following traffic overtake.

q: You're driving along a road with a series of road humps and chicanes. What should you do?
options: Slow down for each hump, then speed up
Drive at the speed limit between features
Swerve around the humps to avoid them
Keep a reduced speed along the whole stretch
explain: Traffic-calming features such as road humps, chicanes and narrowings are intended to slow you down. Reduce your speed as you approach them and maintain a reduced speed along the whole stretch of road.

q: You're driving through a traffic-calmed street with narrowings. A cyclist ahead is riding slowly. What should you do?
options: Overtake before the next narrowing
Stay behind and don't overtake here
Sound your horn so they let you by
Pass them as they ride over a hump
explain: Allow cyclists and motorcyclists room to pass through traffic-calming features. You should not overtake other moving road users while in these areas.

q: You see this sign as you enter a residential street. What does it mean?
options: Hump bridge ahead
Uneven road surface ahead
Road humps for the distance shown
Speed cameras for the distance shown
explain: This sign shows the distance over which road humps extend. Reduce your speed and keep it reduced along the whole stretch of road.

q: You're carrying a tall load on your roof rack in a city with trams. How high above the road are tram overhead wires normally?
options: 4.5 metres
3.5 metres
5.8 metres
6.5 metres
explain: Tramway overhead wires are normally 5.8 metres above the carriageway, but can be lower, in which case height clearance markings are shown. Make sure there's enough clearance for your vehicle and any load before driving under them.

q: You're approaching a low arched bridge and see this sign. What does it show?
options: The bridge is closed to traffic
The road narrows on both sides
There's a weight limit on the bridge
The available width of headroom
explain: This warning sign shows the available width of headroom. Check that your vehicle, including any load, can pass safely.

q: It's a dull, overcast day. Visibility is poor, but you can still see well over 100 metres. Which lights should you use so others can see you?
options: Dipped headlights
Rear fog lights
Front fog lights
Hazard warning lights
explain: Use dipped headlights, or dim-dip if fitted, in dull daytime weather to make sure you can be seen. You MUST NOT use fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced.

q: You're overtaking another vehicle at night on an unlit road. When should you change from dipped to main beam?
options: Before you pull out to overtake
As soon as you start to pull out
When you're level with the other vehicle
When you're halfway along its side
explain: Keep your headlights dipped when overtaking until you're level with the other vehicle, then change to main beam if necessary, unless this would dazzle oncoming road users.

q: You're stopped in a long queue of traffic at night and the vehicles behind you have also stopped. What should you do to reduce glare for them?
options: Keep pressing firmly on the footbrake
Use the parking brake, not the footbrake
Switch on your rear fog lights
Switch on your hazard warning lights
explain: In stationary queues, apply the parking brake and, once the following traffic has stopped, take your foot off the footbrake to switch off your brake lights. This minimises glare for road users behind.

q: You're thinking about overtaking a slow vehicle on a single carriageway. Which of these should you make sure of first?
options: There's a suitable gap in front of it
The vehicle behind can follow you past
Your hazard warning lights are on
The driver ahead has flashed their lights
explain: Before overtaking, make sure the road is sufficiently clear ahead, road users aren't beginning to overtake you, and there's a suitable gap in front of the road user you plan to overtake.

q: You've parked at the side of the road and are about to leave your car. What MUST you switch off?
options: The engine, headlights and fog lights
Only the engine, as lights don't matter
Only the fog lights, if they're on
Only the headlights and the radio
explain: If you stop on the roadside, you MUST switch off the engine, headlights and fog lights, and you MUST apply the handbrake before leaving the vehicle.

q: You see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: A hump bridge
A bumpy road surface
Road humps for a set distance
A steep hill downwards
explain: This sign warns of an uneven road. Slow down, and remember that motorcyclists and cyclists may suddenly need to avoid uneven road surfaces.

q: You've started to overtake a car on a single carriageway. What should you do?
options: Move quickly past and don't cut in
Stay alongside until the road widens
Move back in as soon as you're level
Slow down to match the car's speed
explain: Once you've started to overtake, move quickly past the vehicle and allow plenty of room. Move back to the left as soon as you can, but don't cut in.

q: You see this sign on a country road. What does it mean?
options: Two-way traffic straight ahead
Give priority to oncoming traffic
No overtaking
No motor vehicles
explain: This sign means no overtaking. You MUST NOT overtake after it until you pass a sign cancelling the restriction.

q: You're parking a manual car facing uphill next to the kerb. What should you do after applying the handbrake firmly?
options: Reverse gear, wheel turned towards the kerb
Forward gear, wheel turned away from the kerb
Neutral, wheels left straight ahead
Forward gear, wheel turned towards the kerb
explain: When parking facing uphill, park close to the kerb, apply the handbrake firmly, select a forward gear and turn your steering wheel away from the kerb.

q: You're parking a manual car facing downhill next to the kerb. Which gear should you select and which way should you turn the wheel?
options: Reverse gear, wheel towards the kerb
First gear, wheel away from the kerb
Neutral, wheels straight ahead
Reverse gear, wheel away from the kerb
explain: When parking facing downhill, apply the handbrake firmly, select reverse gear and turn your steering wheel towards the kerb. In an automatic, use 'park'.

q: It snowed overnight and your car is covered in snow and ice. Before you set off, what MUST you do?
options: Clear a patch in front of the driver
Clear the windscreen and nothing else
Clear all snow and ice from all windows
Drive slowly until the heater clears it
explain: You MUST be able to see, so clear all snow and ice from all your windows. You MUST also make sure lights are clean and number plates are legible, and you should remove snow that might fall off into the path of others.

q: You have to make an essential journey in snowy weather. Which of these should you take with you?
options: Warm clothing, a torch and a shovel
Your insurance and MOT certificates
A set of spare summer tyres
A full roof box for extra weight
explain: Take an emergency kit of de-icer and ice scraper, torch, warm clothing and boots, first aid kit, jump leads and a shovel, together with a warm drink and emergency food in case you get stuck.

q: You're driving on a road covered in compacted snow and the steering suddenly feels unresponsive. What may this mean?
options: Your power steering fluid is low
There's ice and you're losing grip
Your tyres are over-inflated
The road has just been gritted
explain: If the steering feels unresponsive in snow or ice, this may indicate ice and your vehicle losing its grip on the road. Avoid sudden actions and check your grip by braking gently in a safe place.

q: You're driving in fog and moisture keeps building up on your windscreen. What should you use?
options: Your rear fog lights
Your main beam headlights
Your hazard warning lights
Your wipers and demisters
explain: When driving in fog, use your windscreen wipers and demisters. Also beware of other drivers who are not using headlights.

q: Visibility is good, but another driver has their rear fog lights on. Why MUST fog lights not be used in these conditions?
options: They drain the battery very quickly
They can make the light units overheat
They dazzle others and can hide brake lights
They make indicators harder to see in daylight
explain: You MUST NOT use front or rear fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced, as they dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights.

q: You're waiting to turn out of a junction in thick fog and can't see far in either direction. What should you do?
options: Edge out and wait in the middle of the road
Stop in the correct position and listen
Sound your horn and pull out quickly
Switch on your hazard lights and emerge
explain: Stop in the correct position at a junction with limited visibility and listen for traffic. When you're sure it's safe, emerge positively and don't hesitate in a position that puts you in the path of approaching vehicles.

q: It's foggy and you have no choice but to park on the road. What should you do?
options: Leave your rear fog lights on
Leave your headlights on main beam
Switch off all your lights
Leave your sidelights on
explain: It's especially dangerous to park on the road in fog. If it's unavoidable, leave your parking lights or sidelights on.

q: You see this sign as you approach road works. What does it warn you of?
options: Loose chippings
Falling or fallen rocks
Uneven road
Slippery road
explain: This road works sign warns of loose chippings. Take extra care, especially near cyclists and motorcyclists, as they are vulnerable to skidding on grit and other debris at road works.

q: You see this sign ahead. What should you do before you reach the hill?
options: Select neutral and coast down
Select a lower gear
Speed up to gain momentum
Switch on your fog lights
explain: This sign warns of a steep hill downwards. Select a lower gear before you reach a long downhill slope to help control your speed. Coasting removes engine braking.

q: You're approaching a level crossing that has barriers but no traffic lights. The barrier starts to close. What should you do?
options: Speed up to cross before it closes
Cross if you can't see a train
Stop and wait at the barrier
Drive round the barrier with care
explain: At level crossings without traffic lights, you should stop and wait at the barrier or gate when it begins to close, and not cross until it opens.

q: You come to a level crossing with user-operated gates but no lights. There's a railway telephone beside it. What should you do before crossing?
options: Open the gates and cross quickly
Sound your horn and wait for a reply
Cross if you can't hear a train
Phone the signal operator
explain: If there are no lights, stop, look both ways and listen before you cross. If there's a railway telephone, always use it to contact the signal operator to make sure it's safe to cross, and tell them again when you're clear.

q: You come to an open level crossing. It has a 'Give Way' sign but no gates, barriers, attendant or lights. What should you do?
options: Look both ways and listen before crossing
Cross quickly, as trains will give way
Wait for a signal from the operator
Sound your horn and then cross
explain: Open crossings have no gates, barriers, attendant or traffic lights but will have a 'Give Way' sign. Look both ways, listen and make sure there's no train coming before you cross.

q: The half-barriers at a level crossing start to come down, but you can't see a train. What should you do?
options: Drive round the barriers if it's clear
Stop and wait behind the white line
Speed up to cross before they close
Sound your horn and cross slowly
explain: Half-barriers lower automatically because a train is approaching. You MUST obey the flashing red lights and stop behind the white line. Never zig-zag around half-barriers.

q: You see this sign on a country road. What does it warn you of?
options: A single bend to the left
A double bend, first to the left
A sharp turn into a side road
The road narrowing on the left
explain: This sign warns of a double bend, first to the left (the symbol may be reversed). Reduce your speed before the bends, which can be sharper than they appear.

q: You're driving along a street where trams run in the road. What should you avoid?
options: Driving on top of the rails
Driving in the left-hand lane
Driving close to the kerb
Driving behind a slow bus
explain: Take extra care where trams run along the road. Avoid driving directly on top of the rails, and take care where trams leave the main carriageway so you don't follow them.

q: You need to cross some tram rails on a wet day. What is the safest way to cross them?
options: At a shallow angle
While braking firmly
Along the line of the rails
Directly at right angles
explain: Take extra care when crossing tram tracks, especially if the rails are wet. It's safest to cross the tracks directly at right angles, and cyclists and motorcyclists may need more space to do so.

q: You're driving in a city where trams share the road. How might the width taken up by the trams be shown?
options: By red lines along the edge of the road
By lines of orange cones along the track
By yellow dots or a different road surface
By blue signs placed every 100 metres
explain: The width taken up by trams is often shown by tram lanes marked by white lines, yellow dots or a different type of road surface. You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or route reserved for trams.

q: You want to stop briefly on a road with a tramway. Why must every part of your car be clear of the tram's path?
options: Trams can't steer round obstructions
Tram rails can puncture your tyres
Trams may push vehicles out of the way
Tram wires may touch your car's roof
explain: Don't stop on any part of a tram track except in a designated bay, and make sure all parts of your vehicle are outside the tram path. A tram cannot steer round an obstruction.

q: You're driving along a road with tram tracks. Where should you take extra care?
options: Only at the tram stops
Only where trams have their own lane
Only when a tram is in sight
Where the tracks cross the road
explain: Take extra care where the track crosses from one side of the road to the other, and where the road narrows and the tracks come close to the kerb.

q: You're driving at night along a street in a built-up area with street lighting. Which lights should you use?
options: Dipped headlights
Sidelights only
Main beam headlights
Front fog lights
explain: You should use dipped headlights, or dim-dip if fitted, at night in built-up areas to make sure you can be seen.

q: You're driving on a very hot day and the road surface has become soft. What could this affect?
options: Your headlight aim
Your speedometer accuracy
Your steering and braking
Your fuel gauge reading
explain: In hot weather the road surface may become soft, or slippery if it rains after a dry spell. These conditions could affect your steering and braking.

q: You come to a level crossing with user-operated gates. The green light is showing. What should you do?
options: Open the gate on your side and drive across
Wait for a railway worker to open the gates
Cross, then leave the gates open for others
Open both gates, check the light, cross quickly
explain: Open the gates or barriers on both sides of the crossing, check the green light is still on and cross quickly. Close the gates or barriers when you're clear of the crossing.
